name: Li I
bio: Li I, who died in AD 827, was a T’ang poet. His poem here is the lament of a favourite who has lost the Emperor’s attention.
The poems here are Herbert A. Giles’s versions in Chinese Poetry in English Verse (1898), given with the poet’s name as spelled in that book.

poems.title: A Cast-Off Favourite
poems.author: Li I
poems.text:
The dewdrops gleam on bright spring flowers whose scent is borne along;
Beneath the moon the palace rings with sounds of lute and song.
It seems that the clepsydra has been filled up with the sea,
To make the long long night appear an endless night to me!

poems.title: An Autumn Evening in the Garden
poems.author: Li I
poems.text:
The Summer's gone, but summer heat remains,
  And sleepless nights still leave us all repining;
So to the garden I have moved my couch,
  And on it I am peacefully reclining.

The white clouds spread themselves across the sky,
  And through the rifts the moon's soft light is falling
On dewy grass and flowers and trees around,
  While from the towers night birds are faintly calling.

The gentle rustling of the tall bamboos
  In subtle symphony of tone is blending
With the waters of the fountain and the brook,
  Which flow and murmur on their ways unending.

While through the gauzy garments which I wear
  The cooling evening breeze is gently blowing,
My feeling of contentment is more deep
  Than when I'm where the ruby wine is flowing.

poems.title: A Song of the Southern River
poems.author: Li I
poems.translator: trans. Witter Bynner and Kiang Kang-hu (1929)
poems.text:
Since I married the merchant of Ch'ü-t'ang
He has failed each day to keep his word. . . .
Had I thought how regular the tide is,
I might rather have chosen a river-boy.

poems.title: On Hearing a Flute at Night from the Wall of Shou-hsiang
poems.author: Li I
poems.translator: trans. Witter Bynner and Kiang Kang-hu (1929)
poems.text:
The sand below the border-mountain lies like snow,
And the moon like frost beyond the city-wall,
And someone somewhere, playing a flute,
Has made the soldiers homesick all night long.

poems.title: A Brief but Happy Meeting with My Brother-in-Law
poems.author: Li I
poems.translator: trans. Witter Bynner and Kiang Kang-hu (1929)
poems.text:
After these ten torn wearisome years
We have met again. We were both so changed
That hearing first your surname, I thought you a stranger —
Then hearing your given name, I remembered your young face
All that has happened with the tides
We have told and told till the evening bell. . . .
Tomorrow you journey to Yo-chou,
Leaving autumn between us, peak after peak.

poems.title: 夜上受降城聞笛 (Ye shang shou xiang cheng wen di)
poems.author: Li I
poems.collection: 唐詩三百首 (Three Hundred Tang Poems)
poems.text:
回樂烽前沙似雪，受降城外月如霜。
不知何處吹蘆管，一夜徵人盡望鄉。

poems.title: 喜見外弟又言別 (Xi jian wai di you yan bie)
poems.author: Li I
poems.collection: 唐詩三百首 (Three Hundred Tang Poems)
poems.text:
十年離亂後，長大一相逢。
問姓驚初見，稱名憶舊容。
別來滄海事，語罷暮天鍾。
明日巴陵道，秋山又幾重。

poems.title: 江南曲 (Jiang nan qu)
poems.author: Li I
poems.collection: 唐詩三百首 (Three Hundred Tang Poems)
poems.text:
嫁得瞿塘賈，朝朝誤妾期。
早知潮有信，嫁與弄潮兒。
